claim: Pur-alpha-deficient mice die after birth with pleiotropic neuronal defects.
source: Pur-alpha-deficient mice die after birth with pleiotropic neuronal defects.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Pur-alpha binds DNA and RNA in the same way.
source: Consistent with the crystal structure, biochemical and NMR data indicate that Pur-alpha binds DNA and RNA in the same way, suggesting binding modes for tri- and hexanucleotide-repeat RNAs in two neurodegenerative RNAopathies.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical assays (EMSA, fluorescence polarization), NMR titration experiments, and crystal structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure offers a molecular explanation for the effect of point mutations in the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
source: It reveals base-specific recognition and offers a molecular explanation for the effect of point mutations in the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
evidence: The crystal structure is used to model and explain the effects of disease-causing mutations, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: A highly conserved phenylalanine is important for Pur-alpha's unwinding and neuroprotective function.
source: Complementing in vivo analyses in Drosophila demonstrated the importance of a highly conserved phenylalanine for Pur-alpha's unwinding and neuroprotective function.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro unwinding assays and in vivo Drosophila rescue experiments with the F II mutant.

claim: Pur-alpha-deficient mice appear normal at birth but develop severe neurological abnormalities after 2 weeks and die shortly after birth.
source: Pur-alpha-deficient mice appear normal at birth but develop severe neurological abnormalities after 2 weeks and die shortly after birth (Hokkanen et al., 2012; Khalili et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pur-alpha-deficient mice show fewer cells in the brain cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum as a consequence of decreased proliferation of the precursor cells.
source: These mice show fewer cells in the brain cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum as a consequence of decreased proliferation of the precursor cells.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings, implicitly supported by the citations in the preceding sentence.

claim: Pur-alpha co-localizes with Staufen and FMRP.
source: Further studies indicated that Pur-alpha co-localizes with Staufen and FMRP and that Pur-alpha (-/-) mice display dendritic mislocalization of both proteins (Johnson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha (-/-) mice display dendritic mislocalization of Staufen and FMRP.
source: Further studies indicated that Pur-alpha co-localizes with Staufen and FMRP and that Pur-alpha (-/-) mice display dendritic mislocalization of both proteins (Johnson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Point mutations in the human Pur-alpha gene cause the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
source: In support of its important neuronal function, point mutations in the human Pur-alpha gene have been found to cause the so-called 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome, which is characterized by neonatal hypotonia, encephalopathy, and severe developmental delay (Lalani et al., 2014; Hunt et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome is characterized by neonatal hypotonia, encephalopathy, and severe developmental delay.
source: In support of its important neuronal function, point mutations in the human Pur-alpha gene have been found to cause the so-called 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome, which is characterized by neonatal hypotonia, encephalopathy, and severe developmental delay (Lalani et al., 2014; Hunt et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pur-alpha is an ubiquitously expressed, multifunctional protein that binds to both DNA and RNA.
source: Pur-alpha is an ubiquitously expressed, multifunctional protein that binds to both DNA and RNA and is known to regulate replication, transcription, and translation (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: Pur-alpha regulates replication, transcription, and translation.
source: Pur-alpha is an ubiquitously expressed, multifunctional protein that binds to both DNA and RNA and is known to regulate replication, transcription, and translation (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: Pur-alpha binds to single- and double-stranded nucleic acids that contain GGN motifs.
source: It has been shown that Pur-alpha binds to single- and double-stranded nucleic acids that contain GGN motifs.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings, implicitly supported by the context and citations in the surrounding text.

claim: GGN motifs are found at origins of DNA replication and enhancers of TATA-box lacking genes, such as c-myc or the myelin-basic protein.
source: Such regions are found at origins of DNA replication and enhancers of TATA-box lacking genes, such as c-myc or the myelin-basic protein, which Pur-alpha regulates.
evidence: This is a statement about known genomic features, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Pur-alpha regulates c-myc and myelin-basic protein genes.
source: Such regions are found at origins of DNA replication and enhancers of TATA-box lacking genes, such as c-myc or the myelin-basic protein, which Pur-alpha regulates.
evidence: This is implicitly supported by the context and previous citations.

claim: Pur-alpha has been routinely purified from cytoplasmic kinesin-containing ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs).
source: Pur-alpha has also been routinely purified from cytoplasmic kinesin-containing ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) (Kanai et al., 2004; Ohashi et al., 2000), further supporting its role in mRNA localization and showing that Pur-alpha is a core factor in localizing mRNPs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pur-alpha is a core factor in localizing mRNPs.
source: Pur-alpha has also been routinely purified from cytoplasmic kinesin-containing ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) (Kanai et al., 2004; Ohashi et al., 2000), further supporting its role in mRNA localization and showing that Pur-alpha is a core factor in localizing mRNPs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the purification data cited.

claim: Pur-alpha possesses dsDNA-destabilizing activity in an ATP-independent fashion.
source: Besides its ability to bind RNA and DNA, Pur-alpha possesses dsDNA-destabilizing activity in an ATP-independent fashion (Darbinian et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha's dsDNA-destabilizing activity is important for DNA replication and transcription regulation.
source: This function has been suggested as important for DNA replication and transcription regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on previous suggestions.

claim: Pur-alpha, being a transcription activator, contacts the purine-rich strand of promoter regions and displaces the pyrimidine-rich strand.
source: It was postulated that Pur-alpha, being a transcription activator, contacts the purine-rich strand of promoter regions and displaces the pyrimidine-rich strand, which would allow the binding of other proteins and activation of transcription (Darbinian et al., 2001; Wortman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a postulated mechanism from previous studies.

claim: The role of Pur-alpha-dependent unwinding activity in RNA localization and in RNA-based neuropathological disorders is currently unknown.
source: The role of Pur-alpha-dependent unwinding activity in RNA localization and in RNA-based neuropathological disorders is currently unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: Rm62 is the Drosophila ortholog of p68.
source: One particularly interesting interaction partner of Pur-alpha is the RNA helicase Rm62, the Drosophila ortholog of p68.
evidence: This is a statement of orthology, which is established knowledge.

claim: Rm62 is implicated in transcriptional regulation, pre-mRNA splicing, RNA interference, and nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling.
source: It is implicated in transcriptional regulation, pre-mRNA splicing, RNA interference, and nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling (Qurashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Nucleic acid-binding of Pur-alpha is mediated by three central PUR repeats.
source: Nucleic acid-binding of Pur-alpha is mediated by three central PUR repeats (Graebsch et al., 2010; Graebsch et al., 2009), which are N-terminally flanked by unstructured, glycine-rich sequences and C-terminally by glutamine- and glutamate-rich regions (Figure 1A; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PUR repeats are N-terminally flanked by unstructured, glycine-rich sequences and C-terminally by glutamine- and glutamate-rich regions.
source: Nucleic acid-binding of Pur-alpha is mediated by three central PUR repeats (Graebsch et al., 2010; Graebsch et al., 2009), which are N-terminally flanked by unstructured, glycine-rich sequences and C-terminally by glutamine- and glutamate-rich regions (Figure 1A; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each of PUR repeats I and II consist of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet, followed by a single alpha-helix.
source: In the recently published crystal structure of Pur-alpha each of both PUR repeats I and II consist of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet, followed by a single alpha-helix (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous crystal structure study.

claim: Repeat I and II fold into an intramolecular dimer that serves as a DNA-/RNA-binding domain.
source: Repeat I and II fold into an intramolecular dimer that serves as a DNA-/RNA-binding domain.
evidence: This is supported by the previous crystal structure study cited.

claim: The third repeat leads to intermolecular dimerization.
source: The third repeat leads to intermolecular dimerization (Figure 1A; Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds to MF0677 ssDNA and ssRNA with similar affinities.
source: (B) Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds to MF0677 ssDNA (left) and ssRNA (right) with similar affinities.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds to CGG-repeat ssDNA and RNA with similar affinity, but less strong than to the MF0677 sequence.
source: (C) Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds to CGG-repeat ssDNA (left) and RNA (right) also with similar affinity, but less strong than to the MF0677 sequence.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Full-length Pur-alpha shows a twofold stronger binding to MF0677 ssRNA when compared to MF0677 ssDNA.
source: (D) Fluorescence-polarization experiments with full-length Pur-alpha and nucleic acids. The full-length protein shows a twofold stronger binding to MF0677 ssRNA when compared to MF0677 ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The affinity for the physiological Pur-alpha target MF0677 is much higher (KD ~200 nM) than for the disease-related CGG-repeat sequence (KD ~2 µM).
source: In these EMSA, the affinity for the physiological Pur-alpha target MF0677 is much higher (KD ~200 nM) than for the disease-related CGG-repeat sequence (KD ~2 µM) (Figure 1B,C; KD estimated from EMSA).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The binding affinities for ssDNA and ssRNA of the same sequence showed no major differences.
source: However, the binding affinities for ssDNA and ssRNA of the same sequence showed no major differences.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Full-length Pur-alpha showed a two-fold preference in binding to MF0677 ssRNA (KD = 0.7 µM) over MF0677 ssDNA (KD = 1.4 µM).
source: Full-length Pur-alpha showed a two-fold preference in binding to MF0677 ssRNA (KD = 0.7 µM) over MF0677 ssDNA (KD = 1.4 µM; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sequences outside PUR repeats I-II moderately affect nucleic-acid binding.
source: Thus, sequences outside PUR repeats I-II seem to moderately affect nucleic-acid binding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the binding of repeat I-II versus full-length protein.

claim: Addition of either ssDNA or ssRNA resulted in almost identical, well-localized chemical shift perturbations of backbone and sidechain amide protons.
source: Addition of either ssDNA or ssRNA resulted in almost identical, well-localized chemical shift perturbations of backbone and sidechain amide protons (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Most NMR signals of residues involved in binding disappeared upon addition of DNA/RNA, pointing toward an intermediate exchange regime.
source: Most NMR signals of residues involved in binding disappeared upon addition of DNA/RNA, thus pointing toward an intermediate exchange regime, which is characteristic for binding affinities in the high nanomolar to micromolar range.
evidence: This is an interpretation of NMR data based on established NMR principles.

claim: The NMR titration experiments indicate identical binding modes of PUR repeat I-II for ssDNA and for ssRNA involving the same residues in both cases.
source: In summary, the NMR titration experiments indicate identical binding modes of PUR repeat I-II for ssDNA and for ssRNA involving the same residues in both cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR titration data.

claim: Crystals of Pur-alpha repeat I-II with a GCGGCGG trinucleotide-repeat ssDNA diffracted to a resolution of 2.0 Å.
source: Crystals of Pur-alpha repeat I-II with a GCGGCGG trinucleotide-repeat ssDNA diffracted to a resolution of 2.0 Å.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the crystallographic data.

claim: The structure was solved by molecular replacement and refined to Rwork and Rfree of 16.3% and 21.5%, respectively.
source: The structure was solved by molecular replacement and refined to Rwork and Rfree of 16.3% and 21.5%, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the crystallographic refinement statistics.

claim: The DNA-bound protein shows the typical intramolecular dimer with two PUR repeats tightly intertwined with each other, forming a globular PUR domain.
source: The DNA-bound protein shows the typical intramolecular dimer with two PUR repeats tightly intertwined with each other, forming a globular PUR domain (Figure 2A; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A and comparison with previous structures.

claim: A superposition of the previously published Pur-alpha repeat I-II apo-structure (PDB ID 3K44) with the structure of the protein-DNA co-complex showed only a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions of 1.14 Å.
source: A superposition of the previously published Pur-alpha repeat I-II apo-structure (PDB ID 3K44) (Graebsch et al., 2009) with the structure of the protein-DNA co-complex showed only a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions of 1.14 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of crystal structures.

claim: When a flexible loop region from residues L107 to K120 was excluded, the RMSD improved to 0.83 Å.
source: When a flexible loop region from residues L107 to K120 was excluded, the RMSD improved to 0.83 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of crystal structures.

claim: No major conformational changes occur in the PUR domain upon nucleic-acid binding.
source: Thus, no major conformational changes occur in the PUR domain upon nucleic-acid binding, which is consistent with the results obtained from NMR chemical shift titrations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural comparison and NMR data.

claim: DNA molecule 1 (DNA 1) is clamped between residues of PUR repeat I and II.
source: In the crystal structure, the DNA molecule 1 (DNA 1) is clamped between residues of PUR repeat I and II (Figure 2A, B; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: PUR repeat II binds DNA 1 with the residue K138 of its β-sheet, and residues N140 and R142 of the short linker.
source: PUR repeat II binds DNA 1 with the residue K138 of its β-sheet, and residues N140 and R142 of the short linker (Figure 2B, C), whereas PUR repeat I contacts the DNA 1 via residues Q52, S53, and K54 in its short linker (Figure 2B, D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: PUR repeat I contacts the DNA 1 via residues Q52, S53, and K54 in its short linker.
source: PUR repeat II binds DNA 1 with the residue K138 of its β-sheet, and residues N140 and R142 of the short linker (Figure 2B, C), whereas PUR repeat I contacts the DNA 1 via residues Q52, S53, and K54 in its short linker (Figure 2B, D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Pur-alpha mainly binds to stacking guanine bases, but also to one of the cytosines (C5) and to the sugar phosphate backbone.
source: Pur-alpha mainly binds to stacking guanine bases, but also to one of the cytosines (C5) and to the sugar phosphate backbone (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Within the crystal lattice the first two bases (G1 and C2) of the 5'-end of DNA 1 are base pairing with the 5'-end of the symmetry related DNA molecule (DNA 1').
source: Within the crystal lattice the first two bases (G1 and C2) of the 5'-end of DNA 1 are base pairing with the 5'-end of the symmetry related DNA molecule (DNA 1'; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cytosine C5 in the middle of the DNA 1 strand is twisted and does not stack with the neighboring guanines.
source: The cytosine C5 in the middle of the DNA 1 strand is twisted and does not stack with the neighboring guanines (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: F145 from the β-sheet of PUR repeat II stacks with the neighboring guanine G4 and thereby blocks the space for the cytosine C5.
source: Instead, F145 from the β-sheet of PUR repeat II stacks with the neighboring guanine G4 and thereby blocks the space for the cytosine C5 (Figure 2E, Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The residues Y57, D59, K61, K70, and R80 of the β-sheet interact with the 3'-end of the second DNA molecule (DNA 2).
source: In the crystal structure, an additional DNA-binding event was observed for PUR repeat I. The residues Y57, D59, K61, K70, and R80 of the β-sheet interact with the 3'-end of the second DNA molecule (DNA 2) (Figure 2B, F; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B and 2F.

claim: The DNA 2-binding interface is similar but not identical to the DNA 1-binding site on PUR repeat II.
source: This interface is similar but not identical to the DNA 1-binding site on PUR repeat II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the two binding sites in the crystal structure.

claim: In PUR repeat I only K61 but not N63 or R65 contact the DNA 2 molecule.
source: However, in PUR repeat I only K61 but not N63 or R65 contact the DNA 2 molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Although there is a conservation of DNA-contacting residues on both PUR repeats, in the crystal structure their modes of binding are not identical.
source: Thus, although there is a conservation of DNA-contacting residues on both PUR repeats, in the crystal structure their modes of binding are not identical.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the binding modes in the crystal structure.

claim: This observation hints toward a potentially asymmetric binding of nucleic acids on both protein surfaces of Pur-alpha I-II.
source: This observation hints toward a potentially asymmetric binding of nucleic acids on both protein surfaces of Pur-alpha I-II.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the structural observations.

claim: Plots of the signal intensities against the protein concentrations yielded a mean saturation at 0.58 ± 0.1 µM (n=3) of Pur-alpha.
source: Plots of the signal intensities against the protein concentrations yielded a mean saturation at 0.58 ± 0.1 µM (n=3) of Pur-alpha (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by filter-binding assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: This indicates a stoichiometric ratio of 1:2 (protein:DNA) and confirms that like in the crystal structure Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds two molecules of ssDNA in solution.
source: This indicates a stoichiometric ratio of 1:2 (protein:DNA) and confirms that like in the crystal structure (Figure 2A) Pur-alpha repeat I-II binds two molecules of ssDNA in solution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the filter-binding assay data.

claim: All amino acids involved in DNA binding within the crystal structure are conserved.
source: All amino acids involved in DNA binding within the crystal structure (Figure 2B) are conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: All mutants showed decreased binding to DNA and RNA oligonucleotides with both motifs, except for Pur-alpha mutant F I.
source: Except for Pur-alpha mutant F I, all other mutants showed decreased binding to DNA and RNA oligonucleotides with both motifs (Figure 3A–E, G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations in PUR repeat I (KNR I, F I) had less severe effects on DNA binding than mutations in repeat II (KNR II, F II).
source: Of note, mutations in PUR repeat I (KNR I, F I) had less severe effects on DNA binding than mutations in repeat II (KNR II, F II).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Pur-alpha has been previously reported to unwind short stretches of dsDNA in an ATP-independent manner.
source: It was previously reported that Pur-alpha unwinds short stretches of dsDNA in an ATP-independent manner (Darbinian et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When the main binding sites on PUR repeat I and II were mutated (QSK I – KNR II) unwinding was abolished.
source: When the main binding sites on PUR repeat I and II were mutated (QSK I – KNR II) unwinding was abolished (Figure 3F, G), most likely due to impaired DNA binding (Figure 3D, G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding assay data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Mutation of F145 (F II) abolished the unwinding activity without a complete loss of DNA binding.
source: In contrast, mutation of F145 (F II) abolished the unwinding activity without a complete loss of DNA binding (Figure 3E–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding assay and binding data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The heterotypic stacking of DNA-bases with F145 in PUR repeat II stabilizes the single-stranded conformation of DNA and enforces a twist of the bases that is important for its unwinding activity.
source: Together these observations suggest that the heterotypic stacking of DNA-bases with F145 in PUR repeat II stabilizes the single-stranded conformation of DNA and enforces a twist of the bases that is important for its unwinding activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural and mutational data.

claim: The structure consisting of two repeat III molecules shows the same overall fold as repeat I-II with an RMSD of 1.5 Å.
source: The structure consisting of two repeat III molecules shows the same overall fold as repeat I-II with an RMSD of 1.5 Å, and only few differences in the amino acid composition of its putative nucleic-acid-binding surface (Figure 4A; Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of crystal structures.

claim: PUR repeat III was previously suggested to mainly mediate dimerization of Pur-alpha.
source: PUR repeat III was previously suggested to mainly mediate dimerization of Pur-alpha (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha repeat III bound with weaker affinities to CGG repeats and to MF0677 than Pur-alpha repeat I-II.
source: We therefore performed EMSA and observed that Pur-alpha repeat III bound with weaker affinities to CGG repeats and to MF0677 than Pur-alpha repeat I-II (Figures 3G and 4B).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figures 3G and 4B.

claim: In fluorescence-polarization experiments, PUR repeat III bound MF0677 ssDNA over 30-times weaker than PUR repeat I-II.
source: Also in fluorescence-polarization experiments, PUR repeat III bound MF0677 ssDNA over 30-times weaker than PUR repeat I-II (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The main DNA/RNA interactions of full-length Pur-alpha might therefore occur via the first two PUR repeats.
source: The main DNA/RNA interactions of full-length Pur-alpha might therefore occur via the first two PUR repeats.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding data comparing repeat I-II and repeat III.

claim: In unwinding assays almost no activity was observed for PUR repeat III.
source: However, in unwinding assays almost no activity was observed for PUR repeat III (Figures 3G and 4C).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding assay data shown in Figures 3G and 4C.

claim: These observations confirm that PUR repeats I-II mediate the main nucleic-acid-binding and unwinding activities.
source: These observations confirm that PUR repeats I-II mediate the main nucleic-acid-binding and unwinding activities and suggest that repeat III might predominantly mediate dimerization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding and unwinding data.

claim: Repeat III might predominantly mediate dimerization.
source: These observations confirm that PUR repeats I-II mediate the main nucleic-acid-binding and unwinding activities and suggest that repeat III might predominantly mediate dimerization.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the binding and unwinding data.

claim: Overexpression of CGG-repeat RNA in the Drosophila eye induces neuronal degeneration and as a consequence the rough eye phenotype.
source: Overexpression of CGG-repeat RNA in the Drosophila eye induces neuronal degeneration and as a consequence the rough eye phenotype (compare Figure 5A with 5B; Jin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Overexpression of Pur-alpha can rescue the eye phenotype in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Overexpression of Pur-alpha can rescue the eye phenotype in a dose-dependent manner, suggesting that this protein is sequestered into the inclusions (Jin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Wild-type Pur-alpha achieved a full rescue of the rough eye phenotype.
source: Whereas the wild-type protein achieved a full rescue (Figure 5C), expression of the QSK I – KNR II mutant failed to ameliorate the rCGG repeat-induced neuronal toxicity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of the QSK I – KNR II mutant failed to ameliorate the rCGG repeat-induced neuronal toxicity.
source: Whereas the wild-type protein achieved a full rescue (Figure 5C), expression of the QSK I – KNR II mutant failed to ameliorate the rCGG repeat-induced neuronal toxicity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A previously reported double mutant R80A/R158A (R I – R II) that impairs nucleic-acid binding was still able to suppress the rCGG repeat-mediated toxicity.
source: On the other hand, a previously reported double mutant R80A/R158A (R I – R II) that impairs nucleic-acid binding (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Graebsch et al., 2009) was still able to suppress the rCGG repeat-mediated toxicity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5E and binding data in Figure 3H.

claim: The mutant F II, which still binds DNA/RNA but fails to unwind dsDNA, is unable to rescue neurodegeneration.
source: Most interestingly, however, is the observation that also the mutant F II, which still binds DNA/RNA but fails to unwind dsDNA, is unable to rescue neurodegeneration (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5F and in vitro data from Figure 3.

claim: These observations confirm the physiologic importance of the nucleic-acid-protein contacts observed in the crystal structure.
source: Together these observations confirm the physiologic importance of the nucleic-acid-protein contacts observed in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo rescue experiments.

claim: These findings formally establish that the binding and unwinding of nucleic acids is required to modulate toxicity caused by pathogenic CGG RNA.
source: In addition, these findings formally establish that the binding and unwinding of nucleic acids is required to modulate toxicity caused by pathogenic CGG RNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo rescue experiments.

claim: Pur-alpha repeat I-II shows strong and specific binding to its physiological target MF0677 DNA located upstream of the c-myc gene.
source: Pur-alpha repeat I-II shows strong and specific binding to its physiological target MF0677 DNA located upstream of the c-myc gene (Bergemann et al., 1992), but much weaker binding to CGG-repeat RNA (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pur-alpha repeat I-II shows much weaker binding to CGG-repeat RNA.
source: Pur-alpha repeat I-II shows strong and specific binding to its physiological target MF0677 DNA located upstream of the c-myc gene (Bergemann et al., 1992), but much weaker binding to CGG-repeat RNA (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The higher affinity for MF0677 (KD ~200 nM) over CGG repeats (KD ~2 µM) is due to differences in sequence and not the absence of the 2' OH group in the DNA.
source: This suggests that the higher affinity for MF0677 (KD ~200 nM; Figure 1B) over CGG repeats (KD ~2 µM; Figure 1C) is due to differences in sequence and not the absence of the 2' OH group in the DNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding data comparing DNA and RNA of the same sequence.

claim: A hydroxyl-group on the 2' position of the pentose ring of the RNA sugar backbone would not cause steric clashes.
source: Finally, the crystal structure of the Pur-alpha/DNA co-complex showed that a hydroxyl-group on the 2' position of the pentose ring of the RNA sugar backbone would not cause steric clashes (Figure 2A,C-F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from examining the crystal structure.

claim: Pur-alpha binds DNA and RNA in the same way and thus will interact equally with both types of nucleic acids in the cell.
source: Together, our biochemical, NMR, and X-ray crystallographic insights indicate that Pur-alpha binds DNA and RNA in the same way and thus will interact equally with both types of nucleic acids in the cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined biochemical, NMR, and structural data.

claim: This is consistent with the previously suggested Pur-alpha-dependent gene regulation by competitive RNA binding.
source: It is also consistent with the previously suggested Pur-alpha-dependent gene regulation by competitive RNA binding (Tretiakova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Previous findings implied that the positively charged β-sheets mediate DNA/RNA binding, whereas the amphipathic helices might contribute to protein-protein interactions.
source: Previous findings implied that the positively charged β-sheets mediate DNA/RNAbinding, whereas the amphipathic helices might contribute to protein-protein interactions (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The crystal structure of the protein-DNA co-complex confirms that the β-sheets, together with their short linkers, are involved in DNA binding, in contrast to the α-helices that show no interaction.
source: The crystal structure of the protein-DNA co-complex confirms that the β-sheets, together with their short linkers, are involved in DNA binding, in contrast to the α-helices that show no interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A comparison of the Pur-alpha repeat I-II apo-structure (PDB ID 3K44) with the co-structure presented here revealed no significant conformational changes.
source: A comparison of the Pur-alpha repeat I-II apo-structure (PDB ID 3K44) with the co-structure presented here revealed no significant conformational changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pur-alpha interacts with nucleic acids by clamping them between its two repeats, mostly by interacting with the guanine bases.
source: In the crystal structure, Pur-alpha interacts with nucleic acids by clamping them between its two repeats, mostly by interacting with the guanine bases (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Only R142 interacts with the cytosine base C2.
source: Only R142 interacts with the cytosine base C2.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: K54 and K138 additionally stabilize the DNA binding by interacting with the sugar phosphate backbone of guanine G4 and cytosine C5, respectively.
source: K54 and K138 additionally stabilize the DNA binding by interacting with the sugar phosphate backbone of guanine G4 and cytosine C5, respectively (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Binding occurs sequence specifically and confirms the GGN-binding motif postulated before.
source: Binding therefore occurs sequence specifically and confirms the GGN-binding motif postulated before (Bergemann and Johnson, 1992).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure and supported by a citation.

claim: Mutation of the interacting residues resulted in a decreased binding affinity and therefore confirmed the interaction sites seen in the crystal structure.
source: Mutation of the interacting residues resulted in a decreased binding affinity (Figure 3G, H) and therefore confirmed the interaction sites seen in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: In fluorescence-polarization experiments, the mutation of KNR I had a less severe effect on DNA binding (KD = 1.3 µM) than mutation of KNR II (KD = 4.1 µM).
source: However, in fluorescence-polarization experiments, the mutation of KNR I had a less severe effect on DNA binding (KD = 1.3 µM) than mutation of KNR II (KD = 4.1 µM; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In the crystal structure all three residues of KNR II make contacts with DNA 1.
source: This is consistent with the observation that in the crystal structure all three residues of KNR II make contacts with DNA 1 (Figure 2B, C), whereas in KNR I only a single amino acid binds to DNA 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The F I mutation in repeat I had a less severe effect on MF0677 ssDNA binding than the F II mutation.
source: Also, the F I mutation in repeat I had a less severe effect on MF0677 ssDNA binding than the F II mutation (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is supported by binding data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: These observations suggest that the MF0677 ssDNA is bound asymmetrically by PUR repeats I-II.
source: In summary, these observations suggest that the MF0677 ssDNA is bound asymmetrically by PUR repeats I-II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutational and structural data.

claim: In FXTAS patients, Pur-alpha binds to CGG-repeat expansions that cause the formation of nuclear inclusions and neurodegeneration.
source: In FXTAS patients, Pur-alpha binds to CGG-repeat expansions that cause the formation of nuclear inclusions and neurodegeneration (Oostra and Willemsen, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha is also incorporated into inclusion triggered by G4C2-repeat RNA of patients with ALS and FTLD.
source: Pur-alpha is also incorporated into inclusion triggered by G4C2-repeat RNA of patients with ALS and FTLD.
evidence: This is implicitly supported by the context and citations in the introduction.

claim: The nucleic-acid binding of Pur-alpha observed in the crystal structure can explain both binding events, as it makes sequence-specific interactions with a GGC motif found in both repeat RNAs.
source: The nucleic-acid binding of Pur-alpha observed in the crystal structure can explain both binding events, as it makes sequence-specific interactions with a GGC motif found in both repeat RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure and the known repeat sequences.

claim: The structural model of Pur-alpha repeat I-II forming a PUR domain has two nucleic-acid-binding surfaces.
source: The structural model of Pur-alpha repeat I-II forming a PUR domain has two nucleic-acid-binding surfaces.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: PUR repeats I and II share the identical binding motif (KNR), and adopt the same fold, despite moderate sequence identity of about ~30%.
source: PUR repeats I and II share the identical binding motif (KNR), and adopt the same fold, despite moderate sequence identity of about ~30% (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Graebsch et al., 2010; Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural comparison.

claim: A stoichiometric ratio of 1:2 for the PUR domain with ssDNA was observed in filter-binding assays.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed a stoichiometric ratio of 1:2 for the PUR domain with ssDNA in filter-binding assays (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by filter-binding assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both binding events appear at overlapping but non-identical surface regions.
source: Both binding events appear at overlapping but non-identical surface regions (Figure 2A, B), which might prefer different GGN-motifs (GGA, GGG, GGC, GGT) as has been previously suggested (Aumiller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure and supported by a citation.

claim: This might explain why CGG repeats bind less strongly to Pur-alpha than the MF0677 sequence, which mostly consists of GGA and GGT motifs.
source: This might also explain why CGG repeats bind less strongly to Pur-alpha than the MF0677 sequence, which mostly consists of GGA and GGT motifs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the binding data and structural observations.

claim: The molecular basis of Pur-alpha's unwinding function has not been understood to date.
source: However, the molecular basis of this function has not been understood to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: The crystal structure of the Pur-alpha/DNA co-complex offers a mechanistic explanation for unwinding: phenylalanine in position 145 of PUR repeat II undertakes base stacking with the guanine G4 and thereby blocks the space for the neighboring cytosine C5.
source: The crystal structure of our Pur-alpha/DNA co-complex offers a mechanistic explanation: phenylalanine in position 145 of PUR repeat II undertakes base stacking with the guanine G4 and thereby blocks the space for the neighboring cytosine C5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cytosine flips out and the 3'-end of the DNA strand becomes distorted.
source: Thereupon, the cytosine flips out and the 3'-end of the DNA strand becomes distorted.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The interaction of K54 and K138 with the phosphate backbone upstream of the cytosine C5 enforces this strong turn.
source: The interaction of K54 and K138 with the phosphate backbone upstream of the cytosine C5 enforces this strong turn (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: F145 is highly conserved throughout different species.
source: F145 is highly conserved throughout different species (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and its mutation (F II) abolishes unwinding of dsDNA (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Mutation of F145 (F II) abolishes unwinding of dsDNA.
source: F145 is highly conserved throughout different species (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and its mutation (F II) abolishes unwinding of dsDNA (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding assay data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Phenylalanine 145 has its structural counterpart in PUR repeat I in position F68.
source: Phenylalanine 145 has its structural counterpart in PUR repeat I in position F68.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural comparison.

claim: Although F68 is also highly conserved, in the crystal structure the guanine base stacking is not mediated by this residue.
source: Although F68 is also highly conserved, in the crystal structure the guanine base stacking is not mediated by this residue.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The conserved Y57 in repeat I stacks with G7.
source: Instead, the conserved Y57 in repeat I stacks with G7 (Figure 2B, F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B and 2F.

claim: The two binding sites of Pur-alpha seen in the crystal structure are asymmetric and might account for sequence-specific binding to nucleic acids with different GGN motifs.
source: As mentioned before, the two binding sites of Pur-alpha seen in the crystal structure are asymmetric and might account for sequence-specific binding to nucleic acids with different GGN motifs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the structural observations.

claim: Expression of pre-mutation CGG-repeat RNA in Drosophila induces neurodegeneration, which is easily detectable in abnormalities in the facet eye.
source: Expression of pre-mutation CGG-repeat RNA in Drosophila induces neurodegeneration, which is easily detectable in abnormalities in the facet eye (compare Figure 5A with 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: While wild-type Pur-alpha rescues the eye phenotype, the RNA-binding mutant QSK I - KNR II failed to do so.
source: While we observed that overexpression of wild-type Pur-alpha rescues the eye phenotype (Figure 5C), the RNA-binding mutant QSK I - KNR II failed to do so (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: A second, previously published RNA-binding mutant (Pur-alpha R I – R II), which showed strongly reduced MF0677 ssDNA binding, was able to fully rescue the eye phenotype.
source: Surprisingly, a second, previously published RNA-binding mutant (Pur-alpha R I – R II), which showed strongly reduced MF0677 ssDNA binding (Figure 3H), was able to fully rescue the eye phenotype (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5E and binding data in Figure 3H.

claim: This observation indicates that arginine 80 and 158 are not required for the binding to nucleic acids important for neuroprotection.
source: This observation indicates that arginine 80 and 158 are not required for the binding to nucleic acids important for neuroprotection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo rescue data.

claim: The loss of rescue by the QSK I - KNR II mutant formally establishes the requirement of nucleic-acid binding for Pur-alpha-dependent neuroprotection.
source: While the neuroprotection by the R I – R II mutant indicates flexibility in nucleic-acid recognition, the loss of rescue by the QSK I - KNR II mutant formally establishes the requirement of nucleic-acid binding for Pur-alpha-dependent neuroprotection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo rescue data.

claim: The F II mutation of Pur-alpha, which abolishes its dsDNA-unwinding activity, also impairs the neuroprotective function in the fly model.
source: Additionally, the F II mutation of Pur-alpha, which abolishes its dsDNA-unwinding activity, also impairs the neuroprotective function in the fly model (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: These findings indicate that unwinding is important for neuroprotection by Pur-alpha.
source: These findings indicate that unwinding is important for neuroprotection by Pur-alpha.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo rescue data.

claim: De novo mutations in Pur-alpha have been found to cause the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
source: Recently, de novo mutations in Pur-alpha have been found to cause the so-called 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
evidence: This is implicitly supported by the citations in the introduction.

claim: Two missense mutations (A89P, K97E) are of particular interest from a structure-to-function point of view.
source: Of the reported mutations (Figure 6—source data 1), two missense mutations (A89P, K97E) are of particular interest from a structure-to-function point of view (Lalani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The residues A89 and K97 of the human Pur-alpha protein correspond to the residues A72 and R80 of the Drosophila protein, respectively.
source: Sequence alignment of Pur-alpha from different species shows that the residues A89 and K97 of the human Pur-alpha protein correspond to the residues A72 and R80 of the Drosophila protein, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: These residues are highly conserved.
source: These residues are highly conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In the crystal structure of the protein/DNA co-complex, A72 does not directly interact with the DNA molecule.
source: In the crystal structure of the protein/DNA co-complex, A72 does not directly interact with the DNA molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A72 forms backbone hydrogen bonds between the β-strands of PUR repeat I to stabilize the nucleic-acid binding β-sheet.
source: Instead it forms backbone hydrogen bonds between the β-strands of PUR repeat I to stabilize the nucleic-acid binding β-sheet (Figure 6A, top) (this study and Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When A72 and its disease-causing counterpart A98 in the human protein are substituted by a proline, the backbone interactions that stabilize the β-sheet very likely become disrupted and thus the protein misfolds.
source: When A72 and its disease-causing counterpart A98 in the human protein (Figure 6A, middle) are substituted by a proline, the backbone interactions that stabilize the β-sheet very likely become disrupted (Figure 6A, bottom) and thus the protein misfolds.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the crystal structure and knowledge of proline's structural properties.

claim: The Drosophila equivalent R80 of the disease-associated human K97 directly binds to the guanine base G7.
source: The Drosophila equivalent R80 of the disease-associated human K97 directly binds to the guanine base G7 (Figure 2B, F and 6B, top) and its mutation results in reduced nucleic-acid binding (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B, 2F, and 6B.

claim: Mutation of R80 results in reduced nucleic-acid binding.
source: The Drosophila equivalent R80 of the disease-associated human K97 directly binds to the guanine base G7 (Figure 2B, F and 6B, top) and its mutation results in reduced nucleic-acid binding (Graebsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: It is conceivable that a mutation of K97 to glutamate impairs nucleic-acid interaction because of repulsive forces and causes dysfunction of Pur-alpha.
source: It is therefore conceivable that a mutation of K97 to glutamate impairs nucleic-acid interaction because of repulsive forces and causes dysfunction of Pur-alpha (Figure 6B, middle, bottom).
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the crystal structure and knowledge of electrostatic interactions.

claim: The reported effect of the K97E mutation in the microdeletion syndrome indicates that nucleic-acid binding by this residue is important at least in humans.
source: Although in our fly model the double mutant R80A/R158A (R I – R II) was still able to rescue neurodegeneration (Figure 5E), the reported effect of the K97E mutation in the microdeletion syndrome indicates that nucleic-acid binding by this residue is important at least in humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the disease phenotype and the fly model data.

claim: The crystal structure of the Pur-alpha/DNA co-complex provides a molecular explanation for the effects of missense mutations in the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
source: Taken together, the crystal structure of the Pur-alpha/DNA co-complex presented in this study provides a molecular explanation for the effects of missense mutations in the 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural analysis of disease mutations.

claim: Wild-type Pur-alpha binds to origins of replication and promoter regions.
source: Wild-type Pur-alpha binds to origins of replication and promoter regions (Bergemann and Johnson, 1992,; Bergemann et al., 1992) and regulates the transcription of more than 20 genes (White et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pur-alpha regulates the transcription of more than 20 genes.
source: Wild-type Pur-alpha binds to origins of replication and promoter regions (Bergemann and Johnson, 1992,; Bergemann et al., 1992) and regulates the transcription of more than 20 genes (White et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pur-alpha's ability to unwind dsDNA might play an important role in the initiation of replication and transcription.
source: Pur-alpha's ability to unwind dsDNA might therefore play an important role in the initiation of replication and transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the unwinding activity and known functions of Pur-alpha.

claim: One recently reported interaction partner of Pur-alpha that might play a role in this context is the RNA helicase Rm62.
source: One recently reported interaction partner of Pur-alpha that might play a role in this context is the RNA helicase Rm62 (Qurashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: It is conceivable that each PUR repeat binds to one of the strands of a duplex DNA molecule thereby unwinding short stretches of dsDNA.
source: Considering that Pur-alpha repeat I-II has two nucleic-acid-binding sites, it is conceivable that each PUR repeat binds to one of the strands of a duplex DNA molecule thereby unwinding short stretches of dsDNA (Figure 7A–C, top).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural data.

claim: The insertion of Pur-alpha between both DNA strands might be achieved through spontaneous breathing of the dsDNA helix.
source: The insertion of Pur-alpha between both DNA strands might be achieved through spontaneous breathing of the dsDNA helix (Peyrard et al., 2009,; Jose et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to previous studies on DNA breathing.

claim: Intercalating residues (phenylalanine, tyrosine) might cause further separation of the two DNA strands via base stacking with the guanines and thereby causing the strong twist of the DNA strands.
source: Intercalating residues (phenylalanine, tyrosine) might cause further separation of the two DNA strands via base stacking with the guanines and thereby causing the strong twist of the DNA strands.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The partly melted duplex DNA could then be further unwound by DNA helicases, which are required for initiation of transcription and replication.
source: The partly melted duplex DNA could then be further unwound by DNA helicases, which are required for initiation of transcription and replication.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on the structural observations and known functions of helicases.

claim: In the crystal structure, base pairing is observed between the 5'-G1-C2 bases of two symmetry-related DNA molecules, indicating that a PUR domain would unwind a short stretch of approximately four to six bases.
source: In the crystal structure, base pairing is observed between the 5'-G1-C2 bases of two symmetry-related DNA molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating, that a PUR domain would unwind a short stretch of approximately four to six bases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the crystal structure the C-terminal end of PUR repeat I-II is located on the opposite side of its nucleic-acid-binding surface.
source: Since in the crystal structure the C-terminal end of PUR repeat I-II is located on the opposite side of its nucleic-acid-binding surface (Figure 7A, B, bottom), it is unlikely that PUR repeat III causes steric clashes interfering with the nucleic-acid binding by PUR repeat I-II.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: It is unlikely that PUR repeat III causes steric clashes interfering with the nucleic-acid binding by PUR repeat I-II.
source: Since in the crystal structure the C-terminal end of PUR repeat I-II is located on the opposite side of its nucleic-acid-binding surface (Figure 7A, B, bottom), it is unlikely that PUR repeat III causes steric clashes interfering with the nucleic-acid binding by PUR repeat I-II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure.

claim: PUR repeat III might only facilitate dimerization, thereby guiding a second DNA-/RNA-binding domain (PUR repeat I-II) to another GGN motif further upstream or downstream on the dsDNA, where additional DNA-unwinding events could take place.
source: Hence, PUR repeat III might only facilitate dimerization, thereby guiding a second DNA-/RNA-binding domain (PUR repeat I-II) to another GGN motif further upstream or downstream on the dsDNA, where additional DNA-unwinding events could take place (Figure 7C, bottom).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural data.
